extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural historians, and travelers using these volumes to analyse or work on Venetian Gothic architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and practical guidance for reading, dating, and designing Venetian Gothic mouldings, traceries, cusps, balconies, and related structural/decorative features. Useful to architects working in Venice or scholars classifying Venetian details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mouldings in various proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: These mouldings are used in various proportions, for all kinds of purposes: sometimes for true cornices; sometimes for window-sills; sometimes, and 3 and 4 (in the Gothic time) especially, for dripstones of gables: 11 and such others form little plinths or abaci at the spring of arches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify moulding profiles and their proportional application (cornices, sills, dripstones, plinths, abaci). Plates and figure references are provided to classify examples; the lower series of profiles (7 to 12 in Plate XV Vol. I) show leaf-ornament on early cornices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byzantine cornice formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some superb Byzantine cornices are of the form having a profile like 16 or 19, with nodding leaves of acanthus thrown out from it, being, in fact, merely one range of the leaves of a Byzantine capital unwrapped, and formed into a continuous line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing Byzantine cornices, look for the continuous unwrapped acanthus-leaf motif—compare arch profiles (Plate V Vol. II) to recognise derivation from capitals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceries as pieces cut from larger composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Venetian tracery is a piece of a larger composition, cut to the shape of the window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether traceries were conceived as an integral, window-specific arrangement (Northern Gothic ideal) or as fragments cut from an extended diaper-like design (Venetian practice). In Venice the latter often results in quatrefoils and foliation being 'cut across' at window edges (examples: Porta della Carta, Casa Cicogna). This treatment may produce grandeur of idea but can 'spoil' the clarity of individual traceries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on color over line
rubrics_metrics.description: They always treated their buildings as masses of color rather than of line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Venetian façades for their colour-mass composition rather than linear emphasis; this explains merciless edge-cutting of traceries and a diaper-like approach to surface ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy of tracery-bar profile
rubrics_metrics.description: In good Northern Gothic the tracery bars are of a constant profile, the same on both sides; but in Venice...one side of a tracery bar is often quite different from the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether tracery bars maintain a uniform profile around interstices (Northern ideal) or vary (Venetian), noting that closure of very small interstices by meeting profiles is a Northern solution, while Venetians often alter or sacrifice profile to allow more light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacrificing tracery bars for light
rubrics_metrics.description: If an interstice becomes anywhere inconveniently small, the tracery bar is sacrificed; cut away, or in some way altered in profile, in order to afford more room for the light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating traceries, look for purposeful cutting-away or profile alteration as a concession to lighting—common in early traceries (examples: bars 1, 2, 5; Casa Cicogna). This is an intended design choice, not merely careless execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sturdiness of tracery bars (structural role)
rubrics_metrics.description: The great sturdiness of the form of the bars...is a consequence of the peculiar office of Venetian traceries in supporting the mass of the building above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Venetian tracery bars not only as decoration but as structural members: thickness, squareness, and added recesses may be deliberate for strength (compare bars 5, 9, 17, 24, 25 and the Ducal Palace tracery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for equal and horizontal pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: The endeavour to obtain equal and horizontal pressure along the whole breadth of the building, not the divided and local pressures of Northern Gothic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess structural systems (shafts, balconies, tracery) for how they distribute horizontal pressure evenly across façades—this principle underlies many Venetian forms and responses to sandy foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balconies as binding/tie-beam elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The balconies...are of great service in knitting the shafts together, forming complete tie-beams of marble, as well as a kind of rivets, at their bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate balcony design for its role in stabilising shafts and providing horizontal binding—look for broad stone bars, socketing/fitting to circular shafts, and metal livetting. Plates and sectional figures (Fig. II/XL) illustrate these masonry details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of oblique-bearing arches in staircases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Venetians seem to have had a morbid horror of arches which were not on a level...rather than introduce the idea of obliquity into bearing curves, they abandoned the arch principle altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging staircases, note whether designers preserved strict horizontality of arches (sometimes at the cost of clumsy or 'valueless' arrangements) rather than using oblique arches or differently profiled bearing curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cusp form (solid vs pierced) and aesthetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The pierced cusp gives a peculiar lightness and brilliancy to the window, but is not so sublime...the narrow cusp occurs also in very early work...The pierced cusp gives peculiar lightness and brilliancy to the window, but is not so sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose or judge cusp types according to desired visual effect: solid, deep cusps produce depth and sublimity (strong shadow); pierced cusps give lightness and brightness. Decorations (shallow trefoil, triangular incision, or a red marble ball) are options for small or large cusps (Ducal Palace cusp as exemplar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Archivolt mouldings produce depth (fifth-order windows)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing the common archivolt mouldings on the projecting edge... we obtain the bold and deep fifth order window...always grand in its depth of cusp, and consequently of shadow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use archivolt mouldings to create pronounced depth, shadow, and visual grandeur; this is characteristic of fifth-order windows used up to the late fourteenth century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return of the cavetto as a dating sign
rubrics_metrics.description: The return of the cavetto in 21, 28, and 26, is comparatively rare, and is generally a sign of later date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence/absence and form of the cavetto (and its 'return') as a diagnostic for dating Venetian details—rarity often indicates later work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle profile variations have large distant effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties of curvature in the trefoiled arches...though apparently slight on so small a scale, are of enormous importance in distant effect; a house in which the joints of the cusps project as much as in 5 c, being quite piquant and grotesque when compared with one in which the cusps are subdued to the form 5 h.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing façades from a distance, pay attention to small profile curvatures and cusp joint projections—minor local differences greatly influence overall character and perceived quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of tracery-bar form to cusp/aperture position
rubrics_metrics.description: The form and character of the tracery bars themselves are independent of the position or projection of the cusps on their flat sides...in every other case the form of the aperture is determined either by a flat and solid cusp...or by a pierced cusp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse whether bar forms are subordinated to cusp/aperture planning (Northern system) or remain independent (Venetian practice). This affects the overall coherence of window composition (example: Porta della Carta is an exception subordinated to Northern system).

rubrics_metrics.name: Roll traceries as dominant Venetian pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in the very early fillet traceries of the Frari and St. John and Paul, Venetian work consists of roll traceries of one general pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify traceries by type: early fillet (rare) vs widespread roll traceries; pattern identification aids dating and stylistic classification (see plate references and specific building examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design adaptation to sandy foundations (stability-led form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The forms of the Venetian Gothic are, in many other ways, influenced by the difficulty of obtaining stability on sandy foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Venetian forms (sturdy bars, continuous balconies, horizontal pressure strategies) as intentional structural adaptations to poor foundations rather than purely aesthetic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural judgement: Gothic (Christian) as ideal over Pagan imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: This architecture, commonly called 'Gothic'...demonstrably the best architecture that can exist; perfect in construction and decoration, and fit for the practice of all time...We must give up [Pagan imitation] totally...and build henceforward only in that perfect and Christian style hitherto called Gothic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the author's normative standard when evaluating architecture: favour Gothic/Christian principles (structural honesty, decoration integrated with construction) and criticise classical/Pagan imitation as 'worthless' and unsuitable for modern practice; use the book's chapters to support comparative judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of detailed moulding evidence to date buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: The above particulars are enough to enable the reader to judge of the distinctness of evidence which the details of Venetian architecture bear to its dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ the plates and enumerated moulding/tracery features as a practical tool to classify and date Venetian buildings—comparative study of profiles, cusps, cavettos, returns, and traceries yields clear chronological evidence.
